title: People Are Always Talking About Me
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article reframes workplace gossip as a largely functional social mechanism, useful for assessing trustworthiness and for keeping behavior in check through the fear of social consequence, rather than as a pure workplace pathology to be eliminated. It then pivots to the risk case: a colleague who, after a real misstep, spirals into believing everyone is constantly talking about and targeting them, reading hostile intent into innocuous remarks. The piece treats that spiral as a leadership responsibility to interrupt quickly, since unaddressed paranoia can drive defensive behavior that makes things worse. Its practical remedy is leader-delivered reassurance and visible support to break the cycle before perception hardens into a self-fulfilling reality.
points: Workplace gossip serves a functional purpose, helping people assess trustworthiness and reinforcing socially acceptable behavior through fear of social consequence.
A colleague who has genuinely erred can spiral into a temporary but real paranoia that everyone is targeting them, reading hostility into innocent remarks.
Left unaddressed, that paranoia can drive defensive behavior that actually worsens the colleague's standing.
Leaders can interrupt the spiral quickly through direct support and reassurance, before the person's distorted perception becomes a self-fulfilling reality.
quotes: So the idea that others are talking about you is a social fact.
Occasionally, however, a colleague who has made a major misstep or faux pas can temporarily come to believe people are talking about them all of the time.
In short order, they begin to read hidden meanings into gestures and innocent remarks. They quickly become paranoid that gossip about them is on everyone’s lips.
When team members are paranoid, even temporarily, they can do and say things they shouldn’t in order to protect themselves.
Just because you’re paranoid doesn’t mean they aren’t out to get you. So said the comedian Woody Allen, mostly in jest.
Good leaders accept that gossip will occur, but they don’t let it create distrust on the part of a valued team member.
